newsitem.title: UK: More regulation urged as key Internet chunks fail.
newsitem.headline: More regulation urged as key Internet chunks fail.

text.p: Concerned Internet service providers, which link computers up around the world, on Friday called for more effective regulation after key chunks of the global computer network earlier failed for four hours.
For many users, electronic mail -- or e-mail -- is the Internet. In theory, any computer can send a message to any other computer in the expanding realm of the Internet.

But on Thursday, millions of electronic messages -- more than an estimated 50 percent -- were returned to senders around the globe and data was jumbled after a software glitch between 0630 GMT and 1030 GMT was compounded by human error in the U.S.
Some Internet companies warned their customers that there could be knock-on effect for some time.
Analysts said the partial failure of the system underlined the fragile nature of e-mail, on which a rising number of both businesses and individuals are beginning to rely for swift communications.

"Obviously this is a major concern and we wouldn't want to see this sort of thing continuing...It's not very encouraging," noted David Hughes, manager IP (Internet Protocol) systems of British Telecommunications Plc.

Hughes said Thursday's outage called into question procedures at Network Solutions Inc, a state-owned U.S. monopoly that is the exclusive registrar for master Internet addresses -- the so-called Domain Naming Service (DNS) ending in ".com", ".gov", ".org", and ".net".
All hundreds of thousands of .net and .com adresses were effectively taken off the air because their data became corrupted.

"I think this raises the question of whether there is a proper accountability mechanism in place -- whether we need more competition or more regulation to stop these sorts of circumstances happening in the first place," said Keith Mitchell, the chairman of LINKS (London Internet Exchange).
LINKS is a non-profit organisation which represents 35 of the largest Internet service providers in Britain.
Although the outage happened during the early hours in America, the Internet is never quiet and ripples were felt around the world as some users were unable to access Web sites.

DNS has been described as "the triumph of the Internet" which has made the system of carrying data over an arbitrary array of computer networks a success. It is effectively an on-line directory -- and is vital to search the network.
But the architecture is designed to have a focal point. Therefore someone has to run it and operate it to effective quality standards, service providers said.
Mitchell said only a limited number of companies should be allowed to use some of the most popular master Internet addresses such as .com (short for commercial).
Mitchell called for more master addresses to be subdivided into country codes to reduce their burden.
"You can never guarantee against anything failing," he said. "But what you can do is you can reduce the scope of the problem."

Mitchell said that although the system could support the size of popular domain names, they caused more of a strain than was absolutely necessary. "Therefore you have to be a bit more careful to stop things going wrong," he said.
Other Internet service providers such as the AIM-listed Easynet played down the problems.

"Naturally any world-wide interruption of the Internet causes concern. But I have enough experience in this marketplace to know that the likelihood of a recurrence of this is minimal," said Easynet's managing director Grahame Davies.
"These incidents are extremely isolated."
